deep.reconstruction: Folio 1v contains no text of its own and no mathematics. The faint writing is mirror-image show-through (bleed-through) of the recto, folio 1r, seen through thin paper. Old repair paper is pasted at the top, the bottom and the left edge. Read in reverse, the ghost lines match the recto transcription line for line: '...untrennbar mit seiner innersten Natur verbunden, wie der Begriff der Zahl. Die Arithmetik, deren einziger Gegenstand dieser Begriff ist, ist schon jetzt eine Wissenschaft von unermesslicher Ausdehnung, und es ist keinem Zweifel unterworfen, dass ihrer ferneren Entwicklung gar keine Schranken gesetzt sind; ebenso unermesslich ist das Feld ihrer Anwendung, weil jeder denkende Mensch, auch wenn er dies nicht deutlich fühlt, ein Zahlen-Mensch, ein Arithmetiker ist.' Even the interlinear insertion 'gar' appears mirrored above its line. The content is therefore the recto's programmatic opening of a draft on the number concept. Its claims are: (1) the concept of number is the most consequential aid the human mind has created and is inseparable from its innermost nature; (2) arithmetic has this concept as its sole object, is already immense, and its development has no limits; (3) its field of application is equally immense, because every thinking person is a 'number-person', an arithmetician. There are no definitions, derivations or computations to reconstruct.
errors: No mathematical errors: the page has no mathematical content.
Codicological point: the verso should be catalogued as blank, showing through from 1r. It should not be treated as a separate text or a second draft.

results.what: Programmatic statement that number is the most fundamental creation of the human mind and that every thinking person is implicitly an arithmetician (show-through of 1r).
results.modern_name: Foundations of arithmetic / philosophical preface on the number concept (logicist-style motivation)
results.usually_credited_to: Dedekind himself. Compare the 1888 preface of 'Was sind und was sollen die Zahlen?' ('der Mensch rechnet immer', echoing the dictum ἀεὶ ὁ ἄνθρωπος ἀριθμητίζει) and the earlier drafts in his Nachlass (e.g. 'Gedanken über die Zahlen', 1872-78, edited by Dugac 1976).
